title: Guam Braces as Powerful Typhoon Champi Nears
summaryZh: 強颱昌鴻逼近關島，當局啟動最高戒備，預料全島停電。
summaryHi: शक्तिशाली टाइफ़ून चैंपी गुआम के पास, सर्वोच्च अलर्ट और बड़े बिजली संकट की आशंका।
summaryEs: El potente tifón Champi se acerca a Guam; máxima alerta y posibles apagones totales.
summaryJa: 強い台風チャンピーがグアムに接近、最高警戒態勢で大規模停電の恐れ。
summaryKo: 강력한 태풍 참피가 괌에 접근, 최고 경계 태세 속 대규모 정전 우려.
summaryEn: A very strong typhoon is passing close to Guam, and officials expect damage and power cuts.
paragraphs: Residents of Guam were bracing for a direct hit or a near miss from Typhoon Champi, which rapidly intensified on Saturday into one of the most dangerous storms to threaten the US territory in years.

By Saturday afternoon, Champi was packing sustained winds of around 140 mph and was expected to peak at 155 mph. Forecasters predicted it would pass just south of the island early on Sunday, local time, but warned that even a slight shift could drag its most violent core across southern Guam.

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero raised the island to Condition of Readiness 1, meaning destructive winds were possible within 12 hours, and urged anyone heading to a shelter to bring a seven-day supply of food and water. US military personnel at bases including Andersen Air Force Base were also sheltering.

The National Weather Service warned of near-total power loss, scarce drinking water and the likely destruction of many homes with metal roofs. Up to 20 inches of rain, waves of up to 35 feet and coastal flooding were also forecast.
Forecasters linked the storm's ferocity to unusually warm Pacific waters and a rapidly strengthening El Niño.
Guam is a small island in the Pacific Ocean. It belongs to the United States. A very big storm, Typhoon Champi, is coming close to it.
The storm got stronger very fast on Saturday. Its winds were about 140 miles an hour. It was going to pass just south of Guam early on Sunday.
The governor told people to stay safe. People who go to a shelter must bring food and water for seven days. Soldiers at the US bases are also staying inside.
Weather experts say almost all homes may lose electricity. There may be big waves, a lot of rain and floods. Houses with metal roofs may break.
Experts say the warm sea is making storms in the Pacific stronger this year.
Guam, a US island territory in the western Pacific, is preparing for Typhoon Champi, which grew very quickly into a dangerous storm on Saturday.

By Saturday afternoon, the typhoon had winds of about 140 miles per hour, and forecasters expected it to get even stronger. It was forecast to pass just south of the island early on Sunday. A small change in its path could bring the strongest winds over southern Guam.

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero put the island on its highest level of alert. She told people going to shelters to bring enough food and water for seven days. US military staff at bases such as Andersen Air Force Base were also told to shelter.
The weather service warned that power could be lost across almost the whole island and that many homes with metal roofs could be destroyed. Up to 20 inches of rain and very high waves were possible.
Experts say warm ocean water and a strengthening El Niño are making Pacific storms more powerful this year.

By Saturday afternoon, Champi was packing sustained winds of around 140 mph and was expected to peak at 155 mph. Forecasters predicted it would pass just south of the island early on Sunday, local time, but warned that even a slight shift could drag its most violent core across southern Guam.

US military personnel at bases including Andersen Air Force Base were also sheltering.

Guam was hunkering down on Saturday night as Typhoon Champi, which had intensified with startling speed, bore down on the US Pacific territory, threatening the island with its most destructive weather in years.

Champi's sustained winds had climbed to roughly 140 mph, with a further peak of 155 mph anticipated. Although its centre was forecast to skirt just south of Guam early on Sunday, local time, forecasters cautioned that a marginal deviation could bring its ferocious core straight across the island's southern villages.

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero declared Condition of Readiness 1, signalling that destructive winds could arrive within 12 hours, and advised those seeking refuge in shelters to bring provisions for a week. Military personnel at installations such as Andersen Air Force Base were likewise ordered to take cover.

The National Weather Service painted a stark picture, predicting near-total power loss, shortages of drinking water and the probable destruction of many metal-roofed homes, alongside as much as 20 inches of rain and waves reaching 35 feet.
Meteorologists attributed Champi's rapid escalation to exceptionally warm Pacific waters, amplified by a fast-developing El Niño.
The US territory of Guam was preparing for potentially severe devastation as Typhoon Champi, having intensified with remarkable rapidity on Saturday, approached the island in the western Pacific.

By Saturday afternoon, the storm's sustained winds had reached approximately 140 mph, and meteorologists projected a peak of 155 mph. While its centre was forecast to pass marginally south of Guam early on Sunday, local time, experts warned that even a minor deviation in its track could expose the island's southern districts to the full force of its core.

In response, Governor Lou Leon Guerrero implemented Condition of Readiness 1, indicating that destructive winds could materialise within 12 hours, and advised residents evacuating to shelters to carry sufficient food and water for seven days. Military personnel at installations including Andersen Air Force Base were similarly instructed to shelter.

The National Weather Service issued a sobering assessment, anticipating near-total power loss, scarcity of drinking water and the probable destruction of numerous homes with metal roofs. Rainfall of up to 20 inches and waves as high as 35 feet were also considered possible.

Scientists have attributed the storm's exceptional strength to unusually warm ocean temperatures, compounded by a rapidly strengthening El Niño, which has made this an extraordinarily active Pacific season.

told.ex: She told me a funny story.

track.ex: The storm's track is hard to predict.

typhoon.en: a very strong tropical storm in the western Pacific
typhoon.ex: The typhoon closed schools and offices.

united.zh: 美國（United States 的一部分）
united.en: part of the name United States; joined together
united.ex: The United States has fifty states.

unusually.ex: It was unusually hot for October.

up.en: used in "go up" (rise) and "keep up with"
up.ex: House prices went up again this year.

urged.en: strongly asked someone to do something
urged.ex: The doctor urged him to stop smoking.

villages.ex: There are many small villages in the valley.

violent.ex: A violent storm hit the coast.

waters.ex: The waters near the coast are warm.

waves.en: lines of moving water in the sea

weather.ex: The weather in Ireland changes quickly.

week.ex: I go swimming twice a week.

were.ex: The shops were closed on Sunday.

western.ex: The western Pacific has many typhoons.

would.ex: A new park would help the town.
